client: I've been so stressed since my partner got laid off last month. I'm the only one bringing in money now, and I keep snapping at them about every little expense, even though I know it's not their fault. Part of me worries that talking about it won't change our financial reality, so what's the point?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy burden of stress and responsibility right now, while also feeling guilty about how it's affecting your relationship. I'm curious—when you notice yourself snapping about expenses, what thoughts tend to run through your mind in that moment?

client: I just immediately think "Here we go again" when my partner mentions spending money. It makes me feel like a failure because I can't provide the way I want to. But then I also get angry because it feels like they don't understand how hard I'm working.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught between feeling inadequate and feeling unappreciated—that must be incredibly draining. What do you imagine your partner might say if they truly understood how much this is weighing on you?

client:
I don't know what my partner would say...that's part of what makes this so hard. Sometimes I think they'd apologize and try to change, but other times I worry they'd just dismiss my feelings as being too sensitive. It's exhausting going back and forth between hoping things will get better and expecting them to stay the same. 

I guess I'm afraid to even bring it up because what if they don't understand? Then I'll just feel worse and more alone than before. It's easier to just keep quiet and deal with it myself.
therapist: It sounds like you're protecting yourself from potential disappointment by keeping these worries bottled up, while also feeling the weight of that silence. How might it feel to share even a small piece of this with your partner, just to test whether your fears match reality?

client:
I get what you're saying, but the thought of bringing this up makes my chest feel tight. What if I open up and they just brush it off or don't understand? That would hurt even more than keeping it to myself. 

I've imagined this conversation so many times in my head, and it never goes well. It's like my brain has already convinced me of the worst possible outcome before I even try.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you'd feel protective of your heart when the stakes feel this high. I wonder if we could explore what makes those imagined conversations go poorly—what specific fears come up when you picture them?

client: I always imagine the worst-case scenarios—like if I open up and they just dismiss me or think I'm being too needy. It's like my brain automatically jumps to rejection before I even give people a chance. The fear of being vulnerable and then regretting it later is really overwhelming.
therapist: It sounds like your mind is trying to protect you from potential hurt by anticipating rejection before it could even happen—that's a very human response to vulnerability. What would it feel like to test this assumption with something small, like sharing just one feeling instead of the whole burden at once?

client: I get what you're saying, but even sharing one small feeling feels terrifying. What if the person reacts badly or doesn't care? I've had that happen before and it just confirmed all my worst fears. The thought of trying again makes my chest feel tight.
therapist: That tightness in your chest tells me how deeply this fear lives in your body—past hurts have taught you to brace for disappointment. What would it feel like to acknowledge that fear while also gently asking: *Is there any tiny part of you that wonders if this time could be different?*

client: I don't know... I get what you're saying, but when I try to imagine things being different, it just makes me more anxious. Like I'm setting myself up to be hurt again. The fear feels so real and solid—it's hard to believe any part of me could see things differently.
therapist: It sounds like your fear feels like a fortress, protecting you from pain but also keeping you isolated—that must feel so heavy to carry. What would it feel like to simply notice that fear, without needing to change it or believe it, just for now?

client: Honestly, just noticing the fear without trying to change it feels... strange. I’m so used to either fighting it or letting it control me. It’s like you’re asking me to just sit with it, and that feels uncomfortable, almost like I’m letting my guard down. What if noticing it makes it worse?
therapist: That discomfort makes so much sense—you're used to either battling your fear or surrendering to it, so this middle path feels unfamiliar and vulnerable. What do you notice happens in your body when you simply observe the fear without either pushing it away or letting it take over?

client: I notice my chest gets really tight and my breathing gets shallow when I try to just observe the fear. It's like my body wants to either fight it or run away, and sitting with it feels unbearable. I don't know if I can actually do this without making the anxiety worse.
therapist: It sounds like your body is sending strong signals that this feels unsafe—that’s important information, not a sign you’re doing it "wrong." What if we honored that resistance by taking it even slower, like noticing the fear for just one breath at a time?

client: I get what you're saying about honoring the resistance, but it’s hard to believe that slowing down even more will help. I feel like I’m already stuck in this loop of fear, and it’s frustrating. What if I just end up focusing on it even more and making it worse?
therapist: It sounds like you're stuck between wanting to try something new and fearing it might make things worse—that frustration is completely valid. What if instead of focusing on the fear itself, we gently shifted your attention to how you’re holding space for it, even in this moment?
